alternatives.tradeoff: Inspectable and easy to back up; search, leases and transactional deletion become bespoke, and the index is rebuilt every launch.

decisions.consequences: A dependency with its own release cadence and migration discipline. FTS triggers must stay in sync with result inserts and deletes, covered by tests. Database and files can disagree after a crash, which the recovery contract resolves.
decisions.reconsider_when: The system SQLite lacks FTS5 on the baseline, in which case GRDB is built against a bundled SQLite, or library sizes make a per-recording file layout with an external index preferable.

decisions.title: Processing runs as explicit state machines with a per-run settings snapshot
decisions.choice: A state machine per processing run over the stages idle, arming, capturing, sealing, recognizing, diarizing, refining, rewriting, noting, delivering and terminal, in the pure core, with a RunManifest written and fsynced at run start pinning mode revision, model installation ids for every model kind the run uses, vocabulary revision, language setting, translation flag, validator pack set and, for reprocessing, the parent result ids and assignment revision. A run visits only the stages its kind declares. Microphone capture starts at the trigger into a pre-roll ring, so arming work runs concurrently with capture rather than ahead of it.
decisions.rationale: Component boundaries follow this sequence. The manifest is what makes settings snapshots real: a run reads its manifest and never live settings, so editing a mode or switching models mid-run cannot change what a result means. The same manifest is what a reprocess copies and mutates, and what recovery reads after a crash. Attaching the machine to a run instead of to a recording is what lets one recording carry several recognitions and several diarizations without ambiguity. Diarization and note generation are stages rather than side effects because they are model-bound, cancellable and interruptible, and any stage without a place in this machine has no cancellation or recovery definition. Starting capture at the trigger removes the case where a push-to-talk user speaks during arming and loses the first word.

alternatives.option: Read live settings at each stage
alternatives.tradeoff: No snapshot machinery; a mode edit during a long recognition silently changes the result's meaning, which the requirements forbid.

alternatives.option: Implicit state through nullable columns
alternatives.tradeoff: Fewer types; illegal states become representable and per-stage cancellation loses its single definition point.

alternatives.option: Treat diarization and notes as post-processing outside the machine
alternatives.tradeoff: Shorter machine; those stages then have no cancellation entry, no recovery transition and no admission accounting, which is exactly the deferral the specification prohibits.

alternatives.option: One state machine per recording
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler list view; a second recognition has nowhere to live and reprocessing has to mutate the recording's state.

decisions.consequences: Every new capability declares where it sits in the sequence and what cancellation there means. Settings changes take effect on the next run, which the interface must show so it does not read as a bug. History shows runs, which is more structure in the detail view than a flat result list. The pre-roll ring holds audio before any mode decision, so cancellation during arming must discard it explicitly.
decisions.reconsider_when: A requirement needs mid-run settings changes, such as switching language during a long meeting, which would need a segmented manifest in place of one per run.

decisions.title: Cancellation contract defined for every stage a run can occupy
decisions.choice: A stage-indexed table of cancellation effects enforced in core and shown in the panel, covering arming, capturing, sealing, recognizing, diarizing, refining, rewriting, noting and delivering, as listed under failure behavior. Cancelling a reprocess run leaves every earlier run's results intact.
decisions.rationale: The specification requires defined effects at every processing stage, and the prior revision left sealing and the meeting stages undefined. Four judgment calls carry the table: sealing runs to completion because it is bounded and idempotent and no disposition is coherent without it; recognizing saves no partial transcript because a truncated transcript that looks complete is more damaging than an absent one; diarizing saves nothing partial for the same reason applied to segment coverage; rewriting keeps the normalized result because the expensive work is done and the user usually still wants their words.

alternatives.option: Cancel always discards everything
alternatives.tradeoff: One rule; throws away a completed recognition because the user did not want the rewrite, which is the most common late cancel.

alternatives.option: Cancel always keeps everything
alternatives.tradeoff: Nothing is lost; a sentence spoken into the wrong window persists to History, which is a privacy surprise.

alternatives.option: Abort sealing immediately on cancel
alternatives.tradeoff: Stops sooner; leaves a half-encoded artifact whose disposition and recovery both need special cases that the idempotent completion avoids.

alternatives.option: Prompt at cancel time
alternatives.tradeoff: No wrong default; a modal on the escape path is when a user least wants a dialog.

decisions.consequences: Workers need checkpoints so cancel is prompt without being abrupt. Cancelling during sealing has a short unavoidable delay while the seal finishes, which the panel names. The panel needs a per-stage message so the effect is visible when it happens instead of discovered later in History.
decisions.reconsider_when: Usage shows repeated re-recording after cancels during recognition, which would argue for keeping partial transcripts clearly marked as partial.

decisions.title: Delivery target latched at arming, with exactly one target per focus outcome
decisions.choice: At arming, latch the frontmost process id, bundle identifier, window number, focused accessibility element and that element's readback capability. At delivery the target is determined once: the latched element when it is still focused; the currently focused element when the latched application is frontmost with a different element focused and the per-mode follow-focus setting is on, which is the default; no target, meaning hold, when follow-focus is off, when another application is frontmost, or when the latched application quit. Re-focusing the latched target is opt-in. Only capture-initiated dictation runs deliver; reprocessing runs never auto-deliver.
decisions.rationale: The intended target is the one the user was looking at when they started speaking, and the panel is non-activating (D-011) so showing it does not disturb the latch. Naming one target per outcome removes the contradiction where policy said follow focus and the insertion mechanism acted on the latched element: whichever element this decision names is the element D-009 writes to, reads back and submits into. Holding instead of inserting into an unexpected application is conservative for a good reason: text placed in the wrong window can be unrecoverable and can be sensitive, while a hold costs one click.

alternatives.option: Always deliver into whatever is frontmost at delivery time
alternatives.tradeoff: No held results; text lands in the wrong application whenever focus changes during processing, which is common on longer recognitions.

alternatives.option: Always act on the latched element regardless of focus
alternatives.tradeoff: One target for every case; writes into a field the user has left, which for a same-window form is the wrong field and is invisible until they look.

alternatives.option: Always re-activate the latched application
alternatives.tradeoff: Matches intent most of the time; pulls focus away from whatever the user chose to do next, sometimes seconds later.

alternatives.option: Always hold and require confirmation
alternatives.tradeoff: Never wrong; adds a click to every dictation, which defeats the tool.

decisions.consequences: The panel needs a held state with actions and History must show undelivered results. The same-application default will occasionally insert into a different field in the same window, which is accepted because it matches clicking into the target field while speaking, and is a per-mode setting for users who disagree.
decisions.reconsider_when: Holds fire often enough to annoy, which would argue for making opt-in re-focus the default for users who enable it, or for shortening processing so focus changes are rarer.

decisions.title: Insertion ladder gated by a content-based confirmation predicate
decisions.choice: Rung 1 sets AXSelectedText on the delivery target named by D-008, inserting at the caret or replacing the current selection. AXValue is never set. Rung 2 writes the pasteboard and posts Command-V. Rung 3 synthesizes Unicode typing capped at 400 characters. Each rung is evaluated by one predicate: the expected text appears at the expected insertion location and the caret or selection sits immediately after it. Confirmed means delivered. An explicit negative, meaning the value is fully readable, byte-identical to the pre-state, and the selection unchanged, is the only outcome that permits the next rung. Any other outcome is unconfirmed: the ladder stops, nothing is retried, and the panel offers Copy and Deliver again. The pasteboard is restored only after a confirmed delivery while the change count is ours, or on the user's explicit action; there is no timer-based restore.
decisions.rationale: RESEARCH distinguishes an accessibility object's value from its selected text and notes that setting an editable field's value can replace its contents, so insertion is a selection-aware operation. It also states that posting a paste event supplies no general acknowledgment that the target consumed the clipboard, so a positive signal must come from reading the target. Comparing lengths or ranges is not that signal: replacing a selection with text of the same length changes neither, which would read as rejection and type the paragraph twice, and an unrelated edit changes both, which would read as success. Comparing content at a location distinguishes those cases and yields an honest third outcome when the content cannot be read. The prior review also established that any fixed restore delay races a delayed consumer, so restore is tied to confirmation or to the user.

alternatives.option: Length or range comparison as the signal
alternatives.tradeoff: Works on targets exposing only a length; produces a false negative on equal-length replacement, whose consequence is duplicated text.

alternatives.option: Pasteboard and Command-V only
alternatives.tradeoff: One path to maintain; always disturbs the pasteboard, including where selected-text insertion would be clean and confirmable.

alternatives.option: Synthetic typing only
alternatives.tradeoff: Never touches the pasteboard; slow for long text, drops characters under load in some targets, and interleaves badly with user typing.

alternatives.option: A dedicated input method
alternatives.tradeoff: The system-supported route for inserting text, avoiding both the pasteboard and event synthesis; requires the user to install and select an input method, changing their typing setup for a dictation feature.

decisions.consequences: Per-application profiles become shipped data with a maintenance obligation and a dated matrix. Some targets will never confirm, so unconfirmed is a normal outcome the interface explains and the pasteboard keeps the transcript until the user acts. Reading a full value back costs an extra accessibility round trip on large fields, which the profile can cap by reading a window around the insertion point instead.
decisions.reconsider_when: The F4 matrix finds a readable signal for targets currently classed unreadable, or a supported API for inserting text into another application appears.

decisions.title: Delivery idempotency, a complete attempt-state table, and no automatic retry
decisions.choice: Commit a delivery_attempts row naming recording, result, run, target and state before any event is posted or any accessibility write is issued. States are pending, in_progress, delivered, rejected, unconfirmed, held, failed and needs_review, with the transitions listed under failure behavior. Terminal states are delivered, unconfirmed, held, failed and needs_review. On launch, pending, in_progress and unconfirmed become needs_review; delivered, held and failed are untouched. The app never re-posts automatically; re-delivery is a user action.
decisions.rationale: Paste into a target that cannot be read back gives no confirmation, so after a crash the app cannot distinguish delivered from about to deliver. Any automatic retry risks inserting the same paragraph twice into someone's document. Committing the attempt before acting means recovery always sees that an attempt was in flight. The prior revision had no success state at all, so a literal reading of its launch rule turned every past success into a review item; delivered is now explicit and terminal, and only genuinely uncertain states are swept.

alternatives.option: Retry pending deliveries on launch
alternatives.tradeoff: Recovers a crash before posting; duplicates text after posting, with no way to tell the cases apart.

alternatives.option: No attempt record, recover from run state
alternatives.tradeoff: One fewer table; the window between deciding to deliver and acting is exactly where a crash is unrecoverable without a durable record.

alternatives.option: Collapse rejected into failed
alternatives.tradeoff: A shorter state list; loses the distinction between a rung that may hand off to the next and an error that ends the attempt.

decisions.consequences: After a crash mid-delivery the user gets a needs_review item and decides. Re-delivery is always explicit, one extra interaction in a rare case. The state table is part of the approved behavior tables and is asserted transition by transition.
decisions.reconsider_when: The confirmable-target class covers the common applications well enough that a bounded automatic retry is safe for those targets specifically.

decisions.title: Recording display as a non-activating panel, with a preview ladder that keeps provisional text
decisions.choice: An NSPanel with nonactivating and borderless style, status-bar level, joining all spaces, movable by background, ordered front without becoming key. Provisional text renders in a secondary style with a live label; the final transcript replaces it in the primary style with a brief change highlight. The waveform is drawn from a 10 ms RMS and peak envelope computed allocation-free on the capture thread. Failures appear as a row with a short reason and one action. Placement is stored as a fraction of the display's visible frame plus the display identifier, clamped to the primary display when either is gone. When the full provisional pass is too expensive or is denied admission, the preview degrades through a ladder that still produces text: a smaller dedicated preview model installation, then longer-interval batched updates at voice-activity pauses. Waveform-only is not an accepted end state.
decisions.rationale: The panel must never become key, since activating it would break the delivery latch that D-008 depends on. Provisional and final text are different artifacts, so they are shown differently instead of silently swapped, and the provisional stream is never persisted as a result. Fractional placement survives resolution and display changes, which is the usual failure of remembered window positions. A provisional live transcript is a named requirement, so a cost problem has to be answered by a cheaper way to produce text, not by removing it; if no rung of the ladder meets the drop-frame and quality bars on the evaluation target, that is a release question for the product owner rather than a silent scope reduction.

alternatives.option: A normal SwiftUI window
alternatives.tradeoff: Standard behavior and less AppKit; it activates the application and changes the frontmost application, breaking delivery targeting.

alternatives.option: Menu bar popover only
alternatives.tradeoff: No extra window; anchored to the menu bar so it cannot sit near where the user is typing, and it dismisses on outside clicks.

alternatives.option: Degrade to waveform and a voice-activity indicator when the preview is expensive
alternatives.tradeoff: Guarantees capture is never disturbed; drops a named requirement, so it is rejected as a design fallback.

alternatives.option: Promote the provisional transcript as the final result
alternatives.tradeoff: Feels faster; delivers text produced from partial context as final, the confusion the requirement asks to prevent.

decisions.consequences: Panel focus and level behavior is AppKit-managed with SwiftUI content and needs its own tests. Users see text change when the final transcript arrives, which is highlighted instead of silent. A preview model installation is a second small model to manage when the ladder's second rung is used, and the panel labels which rung is active.
decisions.reconsider_when: Measurement shows the full pass costs dropped buffers or final-transcript quality, which selects a lower rung rather than removing the preview.

decisions.title: Modes as versioned revisions with structured contracts, a split check set, and a stated disposition
decisions.choice: Every mode carries a structured TransformationContract (allowed operations, an answersQuestions flag, a content bound expressed as a recall threshold or a citation requirement, and the languages its validator supports) alongside its free-form prompt. Revisions are content-addressed and runs pin a revision id. Checks are split: a language-independent set that always runs (expansion ratio, context overlap rejecting spans of eight or more tokens present in context and absent from the transcript, vocabulary survival, script sanity) and a language-dependent set that needs a pack (interrogative survival in order, content-word recall, unsupported-sentence detection). An observed violation in either set retries once with a stricter instruction and then delivers the normalized transcript, retaining the generated text marked contract_violation. When no pack exists the language-dependent checks are unavailable rather than failed: the model runs, the result is retained and marked checks_partial, and the delivered text falls back to the normalized transcript only when the mode declares answersQuestions false and the transcript contains an interrogative marker. Screen and pasteboard context reach the prompt as a capped term list by default, with prose per-mode opt-in.
decisions.rationale: Prompt wording cannot enforce that a dictated question stays a question, particularly when context contains instruction-shaped text, so permitted transformations are a machine-checkable property with a defined failure path. Splitting the check set answers the earlier objection that pack coverage was restricting model use: no model is refused and no output is discarded for want of a pack; what a missing pack changes is which text is delivered, in the one case where the missing check is the one protecting the requirement. Distilling untrusted context to terms is a runtime measure rather than a development-time hope, because it removes instruction-shaped sentences from the prompt instead of detecting compliance afterwards. The claim stops at necessary conditions: these checks can pass on text whose meaning changed, and the adversarial corpus is the standing test of their reach.

alternatives.option: Prompt instructions only, no checks
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest and preserves whatever the model produces; the failure mode is a model answering a dictated question and the answer being pasted into a document.

alternatives.option: Skip generation entirely when no pack exists
alternatives.tradeoff: Uniform conservatism; makes pack coverage a restriction on model use, which the prior review identified as unrelated to the requirement.

alternatives.option: Deliver generated text under partial checks in every case
alternatives.tradeoff: No degradation for multilingual users; removes the protection exactly where the user is least able to check the output themselves.

alternatives.option: Validate with a second model asked whether the output is faithful
alternatives.tradeoff: Catches semantic drift lexical checks miss; costs a second generation pass on the latency path and inherits the same failure mode.

alternatives.option: Pass all context as prose and rely on checks
alternatives.tradeoff: Richer context for the model; leaves instruction-shaped sentences in the prompt with only after-the-fact detection between them and the output.

decisions.consequences: The custom mode editor cannot save a mode without a contract, which is friction the editor makes quick with presets. Thresholds need tuning against the fidelity corpus, and bad thresholds show up as frequent visible fallbacks. Term-list context is less useful to a model than prose, which some modes will opt out of, and that opt-out is recorded on the result. Languages ship with packs one at a time, and the panel states which checks ran.
decisions.reconsider_when: Violation rates stay high on correct outputs, the adversarial corpus finds a violation class that passes every check, or term-list context proves too lossy for the modes that most need context.

decisions.title: Built-in mode set and their contracts
decisions.choice: Four read-only built-in modes, each with an explicit contract. Standard: punctuation, capitalization, optional disfluency removal, vocabulary substitution; no reordering, no summarizing, no answering. Email: Standard plus salutation and sign-off from a template, paragraph breaks, register adjustment, no new factual content, recall-bounded body. Note: adds list and heading structure, recall-bounded. Meeting notes: summarization permitted, bounded by a citation requirement where every bullet references a real segment range and uncited bullets are dropped. All four declare answersQuestions false. English packs ship first; other languages take the disposition in D-012.
decisions.rationale: The specification asks for ordinary dictation plus task-specific output with permitted transformations specified per mode. Meeting notes is the one mode where summarization is the point, so recall cannot be its guard and a citation requirement fits what it is allowed to do.

alternatives.option: One configurable mode with toggles
alternatives.tradeoff: Less to explain; the contract dissolves into a toggle matrix that is hard to check against.

alternatives.option: A larger built-in catalog
alternatives.tradeoff: More coverage out of the box; each mode needs its own fidelity corpus and rubric, and custom modes already cover these.

alternatives.option: Ship an assistant mode that answers dictated questions
alternatives.tradeoff: An obvious use of a local language model; it is the behavior the requirements single out as a hazard, so it would have to declare answersQuestions and be visibly distinct in the mode indicator.

decisions.consequences: Built-ins are read-only; customizing one duplicates it into a user mode carrying the same contract as a starting point, which keeps the built-in fidelity corpus meaningful. Four modes means four rubric corpora per shipped language, scored under the rule in verification.
decisions.reconsider_when: Users routinely duplicate a built-in to make the same edit, which is evidence the built-in should change.

decisions.title: Automatic mode selection: ordered rules, list order as the whole precedence rule, latched at arming
decisions.choice: An ordered rule list evaluated at arming, first match wins, ordered by the user. List position is the complete precedence rule; there is no priority field and no runtime specificity comparison. The editor proposes an insertion position by specificity (URL host plus path prefix, then host, then bundle identifier, then any) and flags rules that can never fire because an earlier rule shadows them. The selected mode is latched into the run manifest. A predicate whose input cannot be obtained does not match, and evaluation continues; if nothing matches, the user's default mode applies.
decisions.rationale: First match on a user-ordered list is the model people know from mail filters and makes conflict resolution inspectable by reading the list top to bottom. The previous formulation mixed first-match with a specificity tiebreak inside an undefined priority field, which meant the list did not tell the user the answer. Moving specificity into the editor keeps its usefulness, as a suggestion at the moment of authoring, without making runtime behavior depend on a comparison the user cannot see. Treating an unobtainable predicate as a non-match keeps a missing permission from producing a wrong mode. Latching at arming means the mode cannot change under the user mid-sentence.

alternatives.option: Highest specificity wins regardless of order
alternatives.tradeoff: No shadowed rules; the user cannot temporarily override a specific rule with a general one, and precedence stops being visible in the list.

alternatives.option: An explicit numeric priority field with specificity as tiebreak
alternatives.tradeoff: Fine-grained control; two ordering mechanisms to reconcile and a list whose display order does not determine behavior.

alternatives.option: Re-evaluate continuously during capture
alternatives.tradeoff: Follows the user across windows; the mode could change mid-sentence and the run would no longer have one manifest.

alternatives.option: Infer the mode from what was said
alternatives.tradeoff: No rules to configure; requires recognition before mode selection, inverting the pipeline and making the current mode unpredictable.

decisions.consequences: The effective mode and whether it came from a rule or the fallback appear in the panel and menu bar for every run. Users reorder rules by dragging, which is the only precedence control. Switching applications mid-recording keeps the mode chosen where the user started, consistent with the delivery latch. Browser URL availability varies and is enumerated per browser instead of assumed.
decisions.reconsider_when: Rule lists grow long enough that manual ordering is unmanageable, which would argue for grouping rather than for a hidden precedence rule.

decisions.title: Vocabulary as staged passes with a defined order around recognition and generation
decisions.choice: Four stages in fixed order. Recognition biasing puts selected terms in the decoder prompt slot, capped to the runtime limit, chosen by mode relevance and recency. Deterministic replacement over the recognition result applies ordered rules, longest match first, boundary-aware using ICU word segmentation for the run's language, case-preserving, non-overlapping, applied once with no cascading. Filler removal is a separate per-mode pass. After generation the replacement table is applied once more and the check set verifies that vocabulary terms survived. Recognition and normalized results are both retained. For scripts without word spacing, replacement uses ICU segmentation where available and otherwise falls back to substring matching with a warning shown in the vocabulary editor.
decisions.rationale: The mechanisms fail differently and must not be conflated. Prompt biasing changes decoding probabilities and guarantees nothing, so the interface says so and never claims that adding a name makes it recognized. Deterministic replacement is exact and belongs on text. The post-generation pass exists because a language model will sometimes normalize an unusual proper noun back to a common word, and the user's spelling should win. Word boundaries are language-dependent, so the boundary rule names its mechanism instead of assuming spaces.

alternatives.option: Replacement only after generation
alternatives.tradeoff: One pass; the generation stage then reasons over text containing mis-recognized terms.

alternatives.option: Replacement only before generation
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler; a model that alters a name in its output goes uncorrected.

alternatives.option: Ask the language model to apply the vocabulary
alternatives.tradeoff: Handles inflection and context that literal matching misses; makes an exact user-specified substitution probabilistic, which is the property users want here.

alternatives.option: Cascading replacement to a fixpoint
alternatives.tradeoff: Handles chained rules; introduces order-dependent results and possible loops for a rarely needed benefit.

decisions.consequences: Two texts per run to store and show. The editor must explain that terms have one probabilistic effect and one exact effect. The prompt slot forces selection when the vocabulary is large, so the panel can show which terms were included.
decisions.reconsider_when: A runtime exposes real biasing or constrained decoding, which moves exact-name handling into recognition.

decisions.title: Context sources: sampled at arming, budget-bounded, digest-only retention, stated ephemeral lifetimes
decisions.choice: Three optional sources sampled in parallel at arming against a 200 ms deadline: focused-element text, selection and window title through accessibility, capped at 4000 characters; one frame of the focused window through ScreenCaptureKit with Vision text recognition, opt-in; the first text item on the pasteboard, capped. Anything missing the deadline is omitted and recorded as omitted. Retention defaults to digest, length and source kind; retaining text is opt-in per mode and deleted with the recording. Transient copies have explicit release points: the screen frame dies when Vision returns and is never written to disk, accessibility and pasteboard text die when the prompt is assembled, XPC buffers are released per credit window, generation key-value state is freed at job end, and no inference service writes prompts or context to disk. In the prompt, context sits inside a per-run random delimiter, labeled reference material, in the form D-012 allows for its source.
decisions.rationale: Sampling once at arming bounds cost and makes a run reproducible; continuous sampling would make the same recording produce different prompts depending on timing. Digest-only retention keeps the library from accumulating copies of unrelated documents and screens while still letting a reprocess report that the original context is gone. Naming the release point of each transient copy is what makes the retention claim checkable rather than a statement about the database only.

alternatives.option: Sample at generation time
alternatives.tradeoff: Fresher context and screen recognition off the latency path; by then the user has often switched windows, so the sample describes somewhere they no longer are.

alternatives.option: Retain full context text by default
alternatives.tradeoff: Reprocessing reproduces the original result exactly; the library accumulates screen and clipboard contents by default, a privacy posture the product should not adopt quietly.

alternatives.option: Continuous screen sampling during capture
alternatives.tradeoff: Captures what changed while speaking; sustained recognition cost and a much larger retention question.

decisions.consequences: Screen recognition may routinely miss the deadline on busy displays and is then absent and noted. Reprocessing a recording whose context was not retained produces a different result, and History shows why. The term-list default means context contributes vocabulary and names rather than sentences unless a mode opts into prose.
decisions.reconsider_when: Screen context proves valuable enough that users want it reliably, which moves sampling off the arming path and makes the rewrite stage wait for it.

decisions.title: Languages: per-mode selection or detection, translation as a derived result of a named parent
decisions.choice: Each mode sets recognition language to an explicit code or to auto. Auto uses the runtime's language identification with its probability; below threshold the run records undetermined, uses the mode's default language, and the panel says so. Translation to English is a separate declared operation producing a result whose primary input names the exact recognition or normalized result it translated. Each model installation declares supported languages, labeled in the interface as declared by the publisher and unmeasured until an evaluation row exists.
decisions.rationale: Recognition quality and rewriting quality are different properties measured by different methods, so they are represented and evaluated separately. Naming the parent result is what makes translation provenance survive a second recognition of the same audio; without it, a translation of the first transcript looks equally like a translation of the second. Marking language support as declared keeps the product from promising coverage nobody measured.

alternatives.option: Always auto-detect
alternatives.tradeoff: Nothing to configure; short utterances and code-switching produce wrong detections and the user cannot pin a language they know.

alternatives.option: Translate by replacing the transcript
alternatives.tradeoff: One text per recording; the original wording is unrecoverable, breaking reprocessing and review.

alternatives.option: Translate as part of the rewrite
alternatives.tradeoff: One pass; translation and formatting become entangled and a failed check cannot separate a translation error from a formatting one.

decisions.consequences: History shows several artifacts per recording and must make the parent of each obvious. A user-supplied model with an inaccurate manifest can overstate coverage, so the interface attributes the claim to the manifest. Rewriting in a language with no validator pack runs and is marked checks_partial under D-012, so multilingual recognition and multilingual checking differ and the interface states which.
decisions.reconsider_when: Measured detection accuracy on short utterances makes auto safe as the default, or a runtime provides per-segment language identification supporting code-switching within a recording.

decisions.title: One ingest port carrying timing and flow control, with a declared format matrix
decisions.choice: All sources implement AudioSource, emitting AudioFrame values that carry stream id, clock domain, presentation time, sequence number, discontinuity flag, native sample rate, channel layout and sample format. Conversion to the canonical 16 kHz mono Float32 recognition input is an explicit stage after the port. Consumers grant credit; a seekable source stops decoding when credit is exhausted, and a live source that overruns drops frames and records a discontinuity instead of buffering without bound. Credit extends across the service connection, so the window queue inside a service is bounded by the same accounting. Microphone via AVAudioEngine, system audio via ScreenCaptureKit, files via AVAssetReader in 30-second windows. Initial matrix: wav, aiff, caf, mp3, m4a in AAC and ALAC, mp4, m4v, mov. Extension: a DecoderProvider port with an opt-in external command-line decoder adapter, off by default, run inside the sandboxed decode service.
decisions.rationale: An untimestamped canonical buffer cannot express what meetings need, which is two native streams aligned by host time with drift and gaps visible, and it cannot express backpressure, which is what actually bounds memory end to end. Windowed decoding bounds the decoder; credit bounds the queue between decoder, converter and recognizer, including across the connection. RESEARCH notes whisper.cpp's example has input-format constraints, so an explicit decoding boundary is needed regardless of which runtime ships.

alternatives.option: Canonical untimestamped buffers
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest consumer code; meeting alignment and gap reporting have to travel around the abstraction, and flow control has nowhere to live.

alternatives.option: Separate live and seekable ports
alternatives.tradeoff: Each expresses its own timing and retry rules; orchestration, cancellation and conversion get duplicated between them.

alternatives.option: Decode whole files into memory
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest of all; a three-hour file at 16 kHz Float32 is roughly 700 MB before any model loads, which the requirements rule out.

alternatives.option: Bundle a general-purpose decoder
alternatives.tradeoff: Every format works out of the box; adds licensing obligations, binary size and a security update duty for a decoder parsing untrusted files.

decisions.consequences: Every source carries timing metadata even when it has one stream and no drift. Live overrun is a visible discontinuity in the recording instead of a silent gap. Canonical conversion discards content above 8 kHz for recognition, so imported originals are kept and meeting streams are sealed at native rate for later use.
decisions.reconsider_when: A speech runtime benefits from a higher input rate, or the credit mechanism proves unnecessary because every runtime consumes faster than any source produces.

decisions.title: Imports are copy-in and commit-late, leaving the source untouched
decisions.choice: Import opens the source read-only, copies it into the session directory, and records a security-scoped bookmark for provenance. The recording row commits only when the artifact is complete and readable. On any failure the session directory is removed and no row exists. Moving the original happens only after commit, as a step the user can decline.
decisions.rationale: A failed import leaves its source unchanged if the import path never opens the source for writing and never deletes it. Committing after the artifact is complete keeps a failure from leaving a History entry pointing at nothing.

alternatives.option: Reference the source in place
alternatives.tradeoff: No duplication; the library breaks when the user moves or deletes the file, and reprocessing later finds nothing.

alternatives.option: Transcode on import and discard the original
alternatives.tradeoff: Smaller library and one decode path; discards information and makes reprocessing with a better decoder impossible.

alternatives.option: Create the row first and fill it in
alternatives.tradeoff: Progress visible immediately; a failure leaves a broken row for recovery to reason about.

decisions.consequences: Imports duplicate storage, visible in the library size view and covered by retention. Large video imports copy the whole file though only the audio track is used; extracting only the audio is a refinement once the cost is measured.
decisions.reconsider_when: Large video imports become common enough that storing extracted audio plus a bookmark beats keeping the original.

decisions.title: Speech runtime: WhisperKit ships, whisper.cpp is the designed second adapter
decisions.choice: Ship WhisperKit from the Argmax Swift package behind SpeechRecognizer, loaded inside the sandboxed speech service with an explicit local model folder and acquisition disabled. Keep whisper.cpp as a designed second adapter behind the same port, built when Intel coverage is required or if F1 or the notice inventory rules the first choice out.
decisions.rationale: Three pieces of evidence in RESEARCH support choosing now instead of deferring. The runtime is distributed as a Swift package and the stated build is SPM, so integration cost is lower than a C API that also needs its own decoding boundary. The WhisperKit model repository states MIT on its card, which is the only positive licensing evidence available for weights the application might offer for download. SpeakerKit ships in the same package, so the diarizer that Meetings requires arrives through one dependency and one acquisition path (D-023). What RESEARCH does not establish is accuracy, latency or long-recording behavior; those are measurements that evaluate the choice, defined by F1 with acceptance ranges in verification, and they are separate from the choice itself. The port keeps the decision reversible at the cost of one adapter.

alternatives.option: whisper.cpp as the shipping runtime
alternatives.tradeoff: Intel and Apple Silicon coverage today with widely available GGML weights; C interop in the hot path, an explicit decoding boundary its command-line example demands, and a second dependency and acquisition path for diarization.

alternatives.option: Maintain both runtimes permanently
alternatives.tradeoff: Maximum flexibility; two parameter translations, two evaluation runs per model update and two descriptor sets to keep current, paid before any evidence says both have a role.

alternatives.option: Defer the choice to a bake-off and build against the port only
alternatives.tradeoff: No commitment without measurement; leaves the model format, the acquisition path and the diarization dependency unsettled while capabilities that depend on them are designed.

alternatives.option: Apple's built-in speech recognition
alternatives.tradeoff: No models to manage; on-device availability and language coverage are controlled by the system and model choice is not exposed, which the requirements demand.

decisions.consequences: Intel is unsupported until the second adapter is built, and the shipped weights are in a format tied to Apple Silicon builds. Results record the runtime that produced them, so a change is visible in History. Until F1 completes, no accuracy or latency claim appears anywhere and the scheduler keeps whole-job restart.
decisions.reconsider_when: F1 misses any of its stated ranges, the notice inventory blocks the weights the app would offer, or Intel becomes a requirement.

decisions.title: Generation runtime: llama.cpp embedded in the generation service, GGUF models
decisions.choice: Embed llama.cpp as a library in GenerationService, loading GGUF models with Metal on Apple Silicon and CPU otherwise, streaming tokens back over the connection. No server binary is used or shipped.
decisions.rationale: RESEARCH records llama.cpp as providing local inference with Metal support and as shipping both library integration material and server tooling, and asks that an embedded worker be compared with a local service including whether network access is possible. Embedding gives control over acquisition and lifecycle, and GGUF reaches the quantized models users already have, which matters because user-supplied models are in scope.

alternatives.option: MLX-based generation
alternatives.tradeoff: Apple-native with good Apple Silicon performance; a different model format, fewer ready quantizations and no Intel path.

alternatives.option: Core ML converted models
alternatives.tradeoff: System-managed execution and no vendored C++; per-model conversion work, and user-supplied models become impractical.

alternatives.option: The llama.cpp server on localhost
alternatives.tradeoff: Reuses upstream tooling; the reachability and forwarding concerns in D-003 apply directly.

decisions.consequences: Vendored C++ with build time, pinning and update discipline. The service is built for target architectures and signed with the bundle. Quantization becomes a user-visible setting with a memory consequence surfaced through D-027.
decisions.reconsider_when: MLX coverage of the quantizations users bring becomes comparable, or measured generation latency on the target is unacceptable and another runtime measurably beats it.

decisions.title: Model identity, immutable content-addressed installs, transactional activation, per-kind checks and recorded notices
decisions.choice: Identity is publisher name, revision string and a SHA-256 over the ordered weight file set. Installation stages into Models/.staging/<uuid>, verifies per-file and set hashes, runs the smoke test for its model kind in the matching service against the staged path, then renames the directory to Models/blobs/<setHash>, a path that never previously existed and is never written again. A single SQLite transaction then inserts the installation row, its per-asset rows with license identifier and retained notice, and updates the active pointer. Compatibility is checked before activation against a per-kind descriptor: speech requires encoder, decoder and tokenizer assets and passes by transcribing a three-second fixture; generation requires weights with an embedded tokenizer and passes by producing 16 tokens from a fixed prompt and seed; diarization requires segmenter, embedder and clusterer assets and passes by returning at least one segment on a ten-second two-speaker fixture. Quality scores never gate activation, and a compatible model with no benchmark row is fully usable and labeled unmeasured. Runtimes receive absolute paths and never load by name.
decisions.rationale: A sequence that spans a filesystem rename and a database update needs an ordering rule, and renaming over a live directory is not atomic. Immutable content-addressed blobs make installation idempotent and leave the only mutable state a database pointer that moves inside one transaction. Hashing weights instead of trusting a name makes the same model checkable across a rename or a re-download. A single generic smoke test cannot catch a diarizer missing its clusterer or a speech model missing its tokenizer, so the descriptor and the test are per kind. RESEARCH warns that a default runtime initialization may download models, so passing explicit paths is the enforcement point, and it asks that the license and revision of each selected model be preserved in the installation manifest, which is why notices are recorded per asset.

alternatives.option: Identity by file name or publisher identifier
alternatives.tradeoff: No hashing cost on multi-gigabyte files; two quantizations under one name become indistinguishable in History.

alternatives.option: Install in place and roll back on failure
alternatives.tradeoff: No staging space needed; a failure during the write leaves a corrupt live model, the outcome the requirement forbids.

alternatives.option: One generic load test for every model kind
alternatives.tradeoff: Less per-kind work; misses missing companion assets, which then fail mid-dictation instead of at install.

alternatives.option: Let the runtime's own downloader manage models
alternatives.tradeoff: Much less code; hands acquisition to a component that may download implicitly, breaking the offline contract.

decisions.consequences: Installation needs free space for the staged and the stored copy, checked before starting. Hashing large files takes time and is shown as a verification step. Blobs can outlive their rows briefly after a crash and are collected at launch. Failed user imports stay in staging with the error attached until dismissed. Assets whose notice cannot be established are importable but never offered for download.
decisions.reconsider_when: Hashing time becomes a usability problem, which argues for incremental hashing during download, or a new model kind arrives whose descriptor does not fit the per-kind pattern.

decisions.title: Meetings: SpeakerKit diarization in its own service, channel origin as fact, attribution as hypothesis
decisions.choice: Record microphone and system audio as separate artifacts with role recorded as a capture fact, aligned by host time, labeled as the microphone channel and the system audio channel. Diarize with SpeakerKit's Pyannote pipeline behind a Diarizer port, running in DiarizationService (D-003), configured explicitly with download disabled, an explicit model folder and explicit segmenter and embedder concurrency, all recorded in the run manifest. Weights are user-acquired through the model store and never bundled. Diarization is a run stage with cancellation and recovery entries (D-006, D-007, D-031) and its output is an immutable diarization result. Per-segment calibrated confidence is stored as unknown and no per-segment margin is stored, because the cited API declaration does not establish either. Centroid cosine distance is retained only where a centroid exists and is used to propose cross-recording identity for user confirmation, never to apply one. Segments correlating with delayed system audio are marked probable echo and excluded from microphone-side attribution. Notes are generated over the timestamped transcript in overlapping windows with per-bullet segment citations, and uncited bullets are dropped.
decisions.rationale: The requirement asks for speaker assignment, editable names and an explicit runtime choice, so the runtime is named: it lives in the package already selected for speech, and RESEARCH documents the configuration flags that keep it from downloading, which is also why it gets its own sandboxed service. RESEARCH establishes that v1.1.0 exposes centroid embeddings with cosine-distance helpers, that a speaker may lack a centroid, and that the declaration does not establish per-segment confidence or margin; the schema follows that boundary exactly rather than assuming richer evidence. A microphone can pick up remote audio from speakers and a system stream can carry several applications, so channel origin is not identity. Cluster numbers are arbitrary across runs, so user-edited names live on identities and assignment revisions (D-037) instead of on numeric cluster identity.

alternatives.option: Diarize a single mixed recording
alternatives.tradeoff: One file and one capture path; discards the channel signal and makes even the easiest question an inference.

alternatives.option: Treat channels as speaker identity
alternatives.tradeoff: Labels users understand immediately; wrong whenever speakers leak into the microphone or several people share a room.

alternatives.option: Store a per-segment margin derived from clustering internals
alternatives.tradeoff: Would give a per-segment quality signal; the cited declaration does not expose one, so it would be an invented number.

alternatives.option: Apply cross-recording identity automatically above a distance threshold
alternatives.tradeoff: Less user work across a meeting series; the SDK defines no universal threshold, so it would attach a name on an uncalibrated number.

alternatives.option: Ship meetings with channel labels only until a diarizer is measured
alternatives.tradeoff: Avoids shipping unmeasured attribution; drops a requested feature, so it is rejected even though the measurement is still owed.

decisions.consequences: Two artifacts per meeting at native rate, roughly doubling meeting storage. Diarization weights are an explicit acquisition step the model manager shows, because notices for the embedder and clusterer are component-specific. Attribution shown as unverified is the normal state, which the transcript view must explain rather than hide. Speakers without centroids get no cross-recording proposal at all. Dropping uncited bullets can remove a correct line that failed to cite, so the drop rate is tracked. F5 inventories the fields actually exposed before the schema is frozen.
decisions.reconsider_when: F5 shows the API exposes per-segment evidence after all, evaluation shows centroid distance is monotone with correctness allowing a derived threshold with its calibration curve, a notice blocks integration and another diarizer takes the port, or mixed-stream diarization matches channel-separated results.

decisions.title: History: append-only results over identified runs, full-text search, tombstones with generation tokens
decisions.choice: History lists recordings, each expandable into its processing runs and their result chains. Search is FTS5 over result text with bm25 ranking and snippets. Playback uses the sealed artifact. Reprocessing creates a run and inserts results; nothing is mutated, and a user-movable pointer selects the displayed run. Deletion sets a tombstone, increments a generation counter and signals cancellation; every worker carries recording id and generation from admission and commits in one transaction that aborts if the row is missing, tombstoned or at a different generation. Hard deletion happens when the last lease releases or at the next launch sweep.
decisions.rationale: A late worker response cannot recreate a deleted recording only if the existence check and the insert are the same transaction; any check-then-insert has a window. The generation counter covers delete-then-recreate at the same identifier. Organizing the list by run is what makes reprocessing through a different speech model or a different diarizer comparable instead of confusing, since each run names the models and mode revision that produced its chain.

alternatives.option: Hard delete immediately and let workers fail
alternatives.tradeoff: No tombstone bookkeeping; a constraint violation becomes the race outcome and scratch files are orphaned.

alternatives.option: Cancel workers and wait for acknowledgement before deleting
alternatives.tradeoff: No tombstone state; the user's delete blocks on a worker mid-window, and a hung worker blocks it indefinitely.

alternatives.option: Overwrite results on reprocessing
alternatives.tradeoff: One result per recording and a simpler list; comparing a new model against the old becomes impossible, which is a stated use of reprocessing.

decisions.consequences: Deleted recordings hold disk until leases release, so the interface says deleting instead of claiming reclaimed space. FTS triggers must handle result deletion, covered by tests. A recording with several runs needs a detail view that makes each run's inputs and outputs obvious at a glance.
decisions.reconsider_when: Result rows dominate database size, which argues for storing older results compressed or on disk instead of inline.

decisions.title: Desktop behavior: menu bar surface, software input gain, and resumption only through an owning player integration
decisions.choice: An NSStatusItem shows state, current mode, recent results and settings. Microphone level is software gain on captured buffers by default, with metering and a clipping indicator; setting the input device's hardware volume is opt-in and restored only if the current value still equals the value the app set. For media, the app uses a MediaPlayerAdapter per supported player: it queries the player's state, issues a pause to that player, observes the transition to paused, and records ownership of that specific pause. Only an owned pause is resumed automatically, and only if the player still reports paused and no other client has changed it. Where no adapter covers the playing application, the app may post a play-pause key when the default output device reports a running client, records the pause as unattributed, and offers Resume playback as an explicit user action for ten minutes. No setting enables automatic resumption of an unattributed pause.
decisions.rationale: The specification states that automatic restoration needs an integration identifying the affected player and confirming the pause transition, and that an opt-in setting does not remove that condition. A device-running flag and a posted media key identify neither the recipient nor the effect, so the previous opt-in automatic resume did not satisfy the condition regardless of its extra checks. Splitting pause from resume keeps the useful half: pausing something unknown costs nothing if nothing was playing, while resuming something unknown can start audio the user stopped by hand. Software gain changes no system setting, so the common case has no restore obligation at all.

alternatives.option: Opt-in automatic resume gated on device idle and elapsed time
alternatives.tradeoff: Nothing to click after recording for any player; the conditions cannot establish which application received the key, so it can resume something the user stopped deliberately, which the specification rules out.

alternatives.option: Private MediaRemote framework for playback state and control
alternatives.tradeoff: Accurate per-application state and precise control without per-player adapters; an undocumented interface that can break on any OS update and complicates notarization posture.

alternatives.option: Do not touch media playback at all
alternatives.tradeoff: Nothing to get wrong; leaves background audio bleeding into recordings, which the requirement asks to address.

alternatives.option: Ask the user each time whether to pause
alternatives.tradeoff: Explicit ownership; a prompt at the start of every dictation defeats the shortcut.

decisions.consequences: Automatic resumption covers only players with an adapter, each requiring its own automation permission and its own maintenance; everything else gets the manual action, which is stated in the menu. A player adapter breaking degrades to the unattributed path rather than to a wrong resume. The clipping indicator surfaces hardware-side clipping that software gain cannot rescue.
decisions.reconsider_when: A supported system API supplies playing-application identity and pause confirmation without per-player integrations, which would extend automatic resumption to every player.

decisions.title: Shortcuts: distinct toggle and push-to-talk bindings, evidence-based stuck-key recovery, no duration cap
decisions.choice: A single ShortcutRegistrar owns a session-level consuming CGEventTap handling keyDown, keyUp and flagsChanged. Toggle and push-to-talk are separate bindings; a combination may be bound to at most one of them, validated at bind time. Toggle acts on keyDown and ignores keyUp. Push-to-talk starts on keyDown and finalizes on keyUp, with an optional per-binding tap-to-lock where a keyUp within a configurable window, 250 ms by default, latches recording until the next press. Lost key-up is recovered from evidence: tap-disabled notifications, screen lock and sleep notifications, and a 1 Hz poll of the physical key state that finalizes when the key reports up while the app believes it is down. There is no maximum recording duration. Per-mode bindings are toggle or push-to-talk bindings with a mode attached. kCGEventTapDisabledByTimeout re-enables the tap. Without the tap, toggle falls back to Carbon RegisterEventHotKey and push-to-talk is unavailable with an explanation.
decisions.rationale: Overloading one binding with a hold discriminator leaves the first hold window undefined and makes a short press ambiguous. Separate bindings remove the ambiguity. Polling the physical key state addresses the real problem, a key-up the tap never delivered, with evidence about that key, while a maximum-hold watchdog would truncate valid speech and act as the recording-duration limit the specification prohibits.

alternatives.option: One binding with a hold discriminator
alternatives.tradeoff: One combination to configure; the first hold window has undefined behavior and a dropped event changes the meaning of a press.

alternatives.option: Carbon RegisterEventHotKey only
alternatives.tradeoff: No Accessibility permission and reliable consumption; no key-up, so push-to-talk cannot exist.

alternatives.option: NSEvent global monitors only
alternatives.tradeoff: Simple API with no tap lifecycle; events cannot be consumed, so the hotkey also reaches the foreground application.

alternatives.option: A maximum hold watchdog
alternatives.tradeoff: Guarantees a stuck key eventually stops recording; truncates a genuinely long push-to-talk recording, which the specification forbids.

decisions.consequences: The app sits on the keyboard event path, so its handler must stay fast or the tap is disabled by timeout, which the re-enable path treats as a monitored condition. Users configure two shortcuts instead of one. The key-state poll runs only while a push-to-talk recording is active. Capture starting at the trigger (D-006) means a very short press still produces a short recording rather than nothing.
decisions.reconsider_when: A supported API provides global hotkeys with key-up, or the poll proves unreliable for remapped or external keyboards, which would argue for a visible stuck-key banner with a stop control.

decisions.title: Model residency under a declared budget covering every model kind
decisions.choice: Budget the application at 8 GB peak on the 16 GB target, counting the app and all its services. At most one speech model, one generation model and one diarization model set resident, each unloaded after ten idle minutes, and admission checks the summed declared or measured footprint against the budget before starting a job. Diarization does not run concurrently with generation under the declared numbers. Activation of a pairing whose footprint exceeds the budget is refused with the arithmetic shown, the refusal stating whether its numbers are measured or declared, and an explicit override available. Once F1 and F5 descriptors exist, admission uses measured peak resident size and Metal heap peak per installation instead of declared file sizes.
decisions.rationale: The specification forbids artificial quotas and requires honest reporting of limits, which differs from ignoring the ceiling: swap on a 16 GB machine turns a latency problem into a system-wide stall. The previous revision counted only speech and generation, so meeting work could load a third model set outside the budget it was supposed to respect. Declared weight sizes omit runtime workspaces, Metal allocations and service overhead, so a refusal computed from them can deny a pairing that would have worked; labeling the basis and keeping the override means the policy never becomes a limit the user cannot see through.

alternatives.option: Load on demand with no residency limit
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest and fastest where memory allows; on the stated target a large pairing plus a browser drives the machine into swap.

alternatives.option: Count only the two large models and treat diarization as free
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler arithmetic; the component whose footprint is least known would be the one outside the accounting.

alternatives.option: Keep selected models resident permanently
alternatives.tradeoff: Lowest per-run latency; several gigabytes held while the app idles in the menu bar.

alternatives.option: Rely on memory pressure notifications alone
alternatives.tradeoff: Adapts to real conditions; reacts after the stall has started.

decisions.consequences: First use after idle pays a model load shown as a loading state. A meeting's diarization and its note generation are sequential rather than overlapped under the declared numbers. Until descriptors exist the budget is arithmetic that can be wrong in either direction, which the refusal text says. Memory pressure notifications still trigger early unload of idle models.
decisions.reconsider_when: Measured residency from F1 and F5 differs materially from declared sizes, or the app runs on machines where the ceiling does not bind.

decisions.title: Egress control enforced by the service sandbox, with the fallback claim written in advance
decisions.choice: Inference and decoding run in services whose sandbox omits the network client entitlement, so the system denies outbound connections. Downloads happen only through ModelDownloader on explicit user action, restricted to an allowlist of model hosts and writing only into staging. Runtimes receive absolute local paths, are constructed with acquisition disabled, and a static check fails the build if a runtime is constructed through an initializer that can download. The external decoder runs as a child of the sandboxed decode service, is off by default, and is disabled entirely by the strict offline setting. The shipped claim is: inference and decoding run in processes the system denies network access, evidenced by an in-service connection attempt that fails, with build checks and a network-denied session as secondary evidence. If F2 shows the sandbox cannot load a runtime by either access mechanism, the fallback is an unsandboxed service for that runtime and the claim for it changes to the exact wording: this runtime runs in a separate process with no networking code in its dependency closure, verified by build check and symbol scan and exercised under a network-denied session, which is weaker evidence than a withheld entitlement.
decisions.rationale: The specification requires that audio, transcripts and context stay on the Mac and that model loading not trigger downloads, and RESEARCH notes a diarization runtime whose default initialization may download models. RESEARCH also states that a scan for socket symbols cannot establish that a process lacks network access and points at signed services with entitlements withheld as the thing to evaluate. An entitlement is a property of the process, so it covers linked frameworks and dynamically loaded code that no scan reaches. Writing the fallback claim now is what keeps a failed access method from silently relaxing the contract: the guarantee text changes visibly and the requirement that data stays on the Mac is still met.

alternatives.option: Symbol scan plus a network-denied session test only
alternatives.tradeoff: No platform dependency and no entitlement work; cannot cover system frameworks or dynamically loaded code, and RESEARCH rejects the scan as evidence of absence.

alternatives.option: Allow runtimes to fetch missing models
alternatives.tradeoff: Better first run with no model manager; makes network access a side effect of loading a model, which the requirements forbid.

alternatives.option: Ship no downloader and require manual placement
alternatives.tradeoff: Strongest guarantee and least code; makes first run considerably harder and pushes users toward downloading models through less careful means.

alternatives.option: Leave the fallback claim to be written if the gate fails
alternatives.tradeoff: Less text now; the moment of failure is the worst time to decide how strong a guarantee to advertise.

decisions.consequences: Entitlement sets become part of the signed product, and a missing one fails closed. The model access path depends on F2, since a sandboxed service needs descriptors or a path exception to read weights. If the fallback applies to any runtime, the interface shows the per-service basis rather than one global statement. The decoder is constrained only if sandbox inheritance holds; if it does not, the decoder stays off by default with the trust transfer stated in its settings.
decisions.reconsider_when: F2 shows the sandbox blocks model loading for a chosen runtime by both access mechanisms, or shows that a spawned decoder does not inherit the restriction.

decisions.title: Processing runs as the provenance spine, with results that can name several inputs
decisions.choice: processing_runs sits between recordings and results. Every result belongs to a run, names its primary input through primary_input_result_id, and records any further inputs in result_inputs with a role. Recognition results are chain roots and carry the speech model installation that produced them; a diarization result is a result kind carrying the diarizer installation; a notes result has the transcript as primary input and rows for the diarization result and prior notes it used. A recording may hold several recognition results and several diarization results, one per run. Results are immutable after insert, enforced by a trigger.
decisions.rationale: A recording cannot have exactly one source transcript while also being re-recognizable through a different speech model, so parentage is a foreign key rather than an inference from timestamps. The single-parent form was not enough once notes entered the graph: a note depends on a transcript and on a diarization result and on an assignment revision, and flattening those into one column would make two of the three invisible to provenance. Adding an inputs table rather than three nullable columns keeps the graph extensible when a later result kind depends on something else.

alternatives.option: Keep one transcript per recording and forbid re-recognition
alternatives.tradeoff: The simplest graph and the shortest History view; removes reprocessing through another speech model, which the requirements ask for.

alternatives.option: Single parent per result, with other inputs recorded only in the manifest
alternatives.tradeoff: Fewer rows and a simpler query; provenance queries cannot join on the second input, so History cannot show which diarization a note used without parsing manifests.

alternatives.option: Fixed nullable columns for transcript and diarization inputs
alternatives.tradeoff: Cheaper joins than a link table; a new result kind with a different dependency needs a migration and another column.

alternatives.option: Attach model ids to results and infer parentage by timestamp
alternatives.tradeoff: No new table; parentage becomes a guess that breaks whenever two runs overlap, which the batch lane makes routine.

decisions.consequences: More joins in History queries and a detail view that presents runs with their inputs instead of a flat result list. Reprocessing gains a clear entry stage, since a text reprocess names its parent result and skips recognition. The FTS index carries results from every run, so search can return two recognitions of the same audio, which the result rows disambiguate.
decisions.reconsider_when: Users never re-recognize or re-diarize, which would make the run table pure overhead, though the same structure is what makes translations and notes attributable.

decisions.title: Crash-safe capture through an fsynced chunk journal with a stated commit order
decisions.choice: Capture writes fixed-period chunks, two seconds by default, of headerless native-rate PCM, each written to a part file, fsynced, renamed, with the directory fsynced. The sealer's cycle per chunk is: encode; append packet bytes to the CAF data chunk; fsync the CAF file; append an index record and fsync it; delete the covered journal chunks and fsync the directory. The index record carries magic, record and chunk sequence, first packet index, packet count, frames per packet, CAF byte offset and length, the per-packet byte sizes as varints, and a CRC32 over the record. The CAF data chunk size is written as -1 during capture and patched at finalization. Recovery accepts the durable prefix of index.log by CRC and by byte range against the file's actual length, truncates to the last accepted record, rebuilds the packet table, and re-encodes surviving chunks.
decisions.rationale: The previous formulation fsynced the index without stating that the bytes it names were durable first, which would let recovery build a packet table over data that never reached disk. Encoded bytes are therefore fsynced before the record that refers to them, and chunks are deleted only after that record is durable, so every step forward is justified by something already durable. Per-packet byte sizes are in the record because an ALAC packet table cannot be reconstructed from a count and an offset. The CRC and the byte-range check are how a torn tail is rejected rather than partially trusted. Asserting instead that a partially written container can be finalized would make recovery depend on an untested property of a format that stores its packet table at the end.

alternatives.option: Write the container directly and rely on it being recoverable
alternatives.tradeoff: No journal, no sealer, no extra fsyncs; the recovery story rests on an untested property of the container format.

alternatives.option: Fsync only the index and rely on ordinary write ordering for the audio
alternatives.tradeoff: One fsync per cycle instead of two; the index can name bytes the page cache never flushed, which is the defect this ordering exists to remove.

alternatives.option: Keep raw PCM as the only durable form until the run completes
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest recovery; transient storage equals the full raw recording, which for a three-hour two-stream meeting is several gigabytes.

alternatives.option: Write a second copy of the container periodically
alternatives.tradeoff: Recovery reads the last complete copy; doubles write volume and still loses everything since the last copy.

decisions.consequences: Two fsyncs per chunk period per stream and a sealer to maintain, plus roughly a 30-second window of journal files alongside the artifact during long captures. Chunk period is the tuning knob between recovery loss and write frequency. Sealing is idempotent, which is what makes recovery from the sealing state safe. If F3 shows reconstruction can be invalid, the structural fallback is to retain chunks until the finalized artifact decodes and hashes, trading journal storage for certainty.
decisions.reconsider_when: F3 shows a loss bound or a reconstruction failure the product cannot live with, or a container format with an incrementally durable index removes the need for a separate journal.

decisions.title: A state-indexed recovery contract with an explicit durability ordering rule
decisions.choice: Every non-terminal run state has an authoritative recovery transition, listed in the data lifecycle and covering arming, capturing, sealing, recognizing, diarizing, refining, rewriting, noting and delivering. Before the sealing commit, ownership and disposition live in the session directory's fsynced manifest, and recovery honors that disposition. The ordering rule is written down: a durable record of intent precedes an externally visible irreversible effect, while a locally idempotent effect is followed by its commit. Recovery may complete deterministic stages such as refining, and never resumes generation, diarization or delivery without user action.
decisions.rationale: A recovery sweep that covers only some states leaves the rest to whichever test author reaches them first, which is the deferral the specification prohibits; the previous revision left the meeting stages uncovered. Naming the ordering rule also makes new stages easy to place correctly instead of case by case. Recording pre-commit disposition in the manifest is what makes a cancellation issued before the History row exists survive a crash.

alternatives.option: Discard any run that was in flight at a crash
alternatives.tradeoff: One rule and no partial state; throws away a completed recognition because the app crashed during a rewrite.

alternatives.option: Resume every in-flight run automatically
alternatives.tradeoff: Least user friction; re-runs generation the user may no longer want and risks re-delivering into whatever is now focused.

alternatives.option: Ask the user at launch what to do with each interrupted run
alternatives.tradeoff: No wrong default; a dialog listing interrupted work at every launch after a crash is a poor first impression and invites blind dismissal.

decisions.consequences: Recovery does deterministic work automatically and stops at anything that consumes a model or touches another application. Behavior tables must cover every state, and the crash-injection suite asserts against them instead of against improvised expectations.
decisions.reconsider_when: A new stage appears whose effects are neither externally visible nor idempotent, which would need a rule of its own instead of a case in this table.

decisions.title: Permissions as a capability-by-state matrix
decisions.choice: A matrix over capability, run state and active adapter replaces any single revocation outcome. Losing microphone or an active system-audio stream terminates capture; losing Accessibility affects insertion, readback and shortcut consumption and not recognition; losing Input Monitoring affects shortcuts; losing browser automation affects URL predicates; losing player automation affects the owned-pause path in D-025; losing Screen Recording ends screen context and system-audio capture while leaving microphone capture running. Denial at launch, revocation during work and restoration each have a defined effect, and restoration is reported once.
decisions.rationale: Mapping every revocation to a capture failure would end a valid recording because the user changed a delivery permission during recognition, and would report a lost shortcut permission as an audio failure. Capabilities serve different stages, so their loss belongs at those stages.

alternatives.option: One global failure state
alternatives.tradeoff: Simple to implement and explain; stops work that is still valid and misreports the cause.

alternatives.option: Ignore revocation until the capability is next used
alternatives.tradeoff: No mid-run interruption; the user gets a confusing failure later with no connection to the change they made.

decisions.consequences: The matrix is longer than a rule, is directly testable, and becomes part of the approved behavior tables. Each capability needs a probe and a change notification path.
decisions.reconsider_when: A capability appears whose loss affects several stages differently enough that the matrix needs a third dimension beyond adapter identity.

decisions.title: One artifact lease protocol after commit, session-directory ownership before it
decisions.choice: A leases table records holder, artifact, acquisition and heartbeat. Acquiring a lease requires the recording row to exist, be untombstoned and match the expected generation. Workers, the audio player, exports and every retention policy acquire leases. Retention skips recordings with a live lease and retries on the next pass. Before the sealing commit no row exists, so ownership is the session directory itself, held by one RunActor, with cancellation and deletion expressed as a disposition value in the fsynced manifest. Discarding audio is a distinct audio_discarded state that disables playback, re-recognition and re-diarization while leaving text reprocessing available. Stale leases are reclaimed at launch and by a sweeper.
decisions.rationale: Giving user-initiated deletion a tombstone and generation protocol while letting age, size and audio-only policies bypass it would let a scheduled policy remove an artifact under an admitted job or during playback. One protocol for every consumer removes the class of race instead of one instance. The prior review noted that the protocol presupposed a row that capture does not create until sealing; naming the session directory as the pre-commit unit of ownership closes that gap without inventing a placeholder row that recovery would then have to reconcile.

alternatives.option: Create a placeholder recording row at arming
alternatives.tradeoff: One ownership mechanism throughout; History gains rows for recordings that may never exist, and every query and sweep must filter them.

alternatives.option: Retention as immediate deletion with best-effort cancellation
alternatives.tradeoff: Policies always run on schedule; a race with an admitted job produces a failure whose outcome depends on timing.

alternatives.option: Quiesce all work before retention runs
alternatives.tradeoff: No leases needed; a long import blocks retention indefinitely, and retention blocks new work while it runs.

alternatives.option: Reference counting in memory only
alternatives.tradeoff: Cheaper than a table; counts vanish on a crash, so recovery cannot tell which artifacts were in use.

decisions.consequences: Every consumer of a committed artifact acquires and heartbeats a lease, including playback. Pre-commit work has a different ownership mechanism, so recovery has two paths to implement and test. Retention can lag when a recording stays busy, which is reported instead of forced.
